title: BALAZ AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
summary:
In the case of Balaz and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were members of the Baláž family, Slovak nationals of Roma origin, residing in Leopoldov. The family, who operated a small entertainment park with movable trailers, alleged that they were subjected to discriminatory and arbitrary police interventions due to their Roma identity. The central harm concerned repeated police stops and alleged ill-treatment, including harsh language and physical mistreatment, as well as a lack of effective investigation into their complaints, which the applicants argued was rooted in anti-Roma bias.

The incidents occurred in September 2001, when Mr. Vincent Baláž Jr. and Ms. Jana Konečníková were stopped by police while transporting trailers without number plates. The applicants claimed that police officers used abusive language, entered their property without permission, and physically mistreated Mr. Baláž Jr. Despite numerous complaints to various authorities, including the police and prosecution services, all investigations concluded that the allegations were unsubstantiated and dismissed the complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and 17 (prohibition of abuse of rights). However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had either not exhausted available domestic remedies or were not considered “victims” under the Convention.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking redress for alleged discrimination and police misconduct, reflecting broader historical challenges of access to justice for Roma and Travellers in Europe.
